claim: MEGF8 is a modifier of BMP signaling in trigeminal sensory neurons.
source: MEGF8 is a modifier of BMP signaling in trigeminal sensory neurons
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, supported by multiple experimental approaches including genetic analysis, expression studies, and functional assays showing Megf8's role in BMP4 signaling in TG neurons.

claim: A three-generation forward genetic screen in mice identified Megf8 as a novel modifier of BMP4 signaling in trigeminal ganglion (TG) neurons.
source: Using a three-generation forward genetic screen in mice we have identified Megf8 as a novel modifier of BMP4 signaling in trigeminal ganglion (TG) neurons.
evidence: The manuscript describes the forward genetic screen methodology and the identification of Megf8 through this approach.

claim: Loss of Megf8 disrupts axon guidance in the peripheral nervous system.
source: Loss of Megf8 disrupts axon guidance in the peripheral nervous system
evidence: Demonstrated through whole-mount neurofilament staining showing defasciculation of TG axons in Megf8 mutants.

claim: Loss of Megf8 leads to defects in development of the limb, heart, and left-right patterning.
source: Loss of Megf8 disrupts axon guidance in the peripheral nervous system and leads to defects in development of the limb, heart, and left-right patterning
evidence: Multiple figures show limb polydactyly, heart looping defects, and left-right asymmetry defects in Megf8 mutants.

claim: Defects observed in Megf8 loss-of-function mice resemble those observed in Bmp4 loss-of-function mice.
source: defects that resemble those observed in Bmp4 loss-of-function mice
evidence: The manuscript compares phenotypes between Megf8 and Bmp4 mutants and provides a table (Table 1) summarizing the similarities.

claim: Bmp4 is expressed in a pattern that defines the permissive field for the peripheral projections of TG axons.
source: Bmp4 is expressed in a pattern that defines the permissive field for the peripheral projections of TG axons
evidence: Demonstrated through whole-mount β-galactosidase staining showing Bmp4 expression pattern relative to developing TG axons.

claim: Mice lacking BMP signaling in sensory neurons exhibit TG axon defects that resemble those observed in Megf8 embryos.
source: mice lacking BMP signaling in sensory neurons exhibit TG axon defects that resemble those observed in Megf8 embryos
evidence: Shown through analysis of Wnt1-Cre;Bmpr2Flox/− embryos which phenocopy Megf8 mutants.

claim: TG axon growth is robustly inhibited by BMP4.
source: TG axon growth is robustly inhibited by BMP4
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro TG explant assays showing dose-dependent inhibition of axon outgrowth by BMP4.

claim: BMP4 inhibition of TG axon growth is dependent on Megf8.
source: this inhibition is dependent on Megf8
evidence: TG explants from Megf8−/− embryos show reduced response to BMP4-mediated inhibition compared to controls.

claim: Megf8 is involved in mediating BMP4 signaling and guidance of developing TG axons.
source: our data suggest that Megf8 is involved in mediating BMP4 signaling and guidance of developing TG axons
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including genetic interactions, expression patterns, and functional assays.

claim: BMP signaling is an important regulator of sensory neuron development.
source: Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling has emerged as an important regulator of sensory neuron development.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on BMP function in sensory neurons.

claim: BMPs are members of the TGFβ superfamily of secreted growth factors.
source: BMPs are members of the TGFβ superfamily of secreted growth factors
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about BMP classification.

claim: BMPs are required for a wide range of developmental functions including gastrulation, mesoderm formation, neural patterning, left-right asymmetry, skeletal and limb development, kidney formation, and heart development.
source: BMPs are members of the TGFβ superfamily of secreted growth factors and are required for a wide range of developmental functions including gastrulation, mesoderm formation, neural patterning, left-right asymmetry, skeletal and limb development, kidney formation, and heart development (Zhao, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao, 2003.

claim: BMP7 in the spinal cord roof plate repels axons of developing commissural neurons.
source: BMP7 in the spinal cord roof plate repels axons of developing commissural neurons thus orienting their growth toward the floor plate (Augsburger et al., 1999; Butler and Dodd, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Augsburger et al., 1999 and Butler and Dodd, 2003.

claim: BMP4 is a target-derived cue that augments development of somatosensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglia (TG) and dorsal root ganglia (DRG).
source: BMP4 is a target-derived cue that augments development of somatosensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglia (TG) and dorsal root ganglia (DRG).
evidence: Supported by subsequent citations to studies on BMP4 function in sensory neurons.

claim: BMP4 is expressed in the developing craniofacial region and signals retrogradely to coordinate differential gene expression and patterning along the dorsoventral axis of the trigeminal ganglion.
source: BMP4 is expressed in the developing craniofacial region and signals retrogradely to coordinate differential gene expression and patterning along the dorsoventral axis of the trigeminal ganglion (Hodge et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hodge et al., 2007.

claim: Altering the level of BMP4 expression in the skin leads to changes in the peripheral innervation and number of sensory neurons found in both the TG and DRG.
source: Furthermore, BMP4 appears to have a trophic effect on TG and DRG neurons as altering the level of BMP4 expression in the skin leads to changes in the peripheral innervation and number of sensory neurons found in both the TG and DRG (Guha et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guha et al., 2004.

claim: Line 687 exhibits defasciculation of trigeminal ganglion axons.
source: A forward genetic screen identifies line 687, which exhibits defasciculation of trigeminal ganglion axons
evidence: Demonstrated through whole-mount neurofilament staining shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Line 687 mutation is located on chromosome 7.
source: Figure 1B shows schematic diagram of the region of Chromosome seven found to contain the Line 687 mutation
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic mapping shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Line 687 mutation is a point mutation in Megf8 (5324T>C).
source: Sequence data highlighting the mutation (Megf8 5324T>C) observed in Line 687 mutant DNA compared with C57BL/6 wild-type DNA.
evidence: Shown through DNA sequencing data in Figure 1C.

claim: The Line 687 point mutation induces a single amino acid substitution L1775P in a Kelch domain of Megf8.
source: The Line 687 point mutation induces a single amino acid substitution L1775P in a Kelch domain of Megf8.
evidence: Shown in schematic diagram in Figure 1D.

claim: Megf8L1775P/Trap embryos phenocopy the Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants and show defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic nerve.
source: Megf8L1775P/Trap embryos phenocopy the Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants and show defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic nerve (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through complementation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Line 687 TG phenotype results from the Megf8L1775P mutation.
source: These results confirm that the Line 687 TG phenotype results from the Megf8L1775P mutation
evidence: Confirmed through complementation analysis with the Megf8Trap allele.

claim: Megf8 is required for proper growth and guidance of the TG ophthalmic nerve.
source: These results confirm that the Line 687 TG phenotype results from the Megf8L1775P mutation and demonstrate that Megf8 is required for proper growth and guidance of the TG ophthalmic nerve.
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic analysis and phenotypic characterization.

claim: Megf8 is expressed widely during development at E8.5, E9.5, and E10.5.
source: Whole-mount in situ hybridization (ISH) for Megf8 at E8.5, E9.5, and E10.5.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount ISH in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Megf8 is expressed in the DRG at E11.5.
source: ISH for Megf8 on E11.5 transverse cryosection shows expression in the DRG.
evidence: Shown through ISH in Figure 2D.

claim: Megf8 is expressed in the TG at E11.5.
source: ISH for Megf8 on E11.5 transverse cryosection shows expression in the TG.
evidence: Shown through ISH in Figure 2E.

claim: Megf8 is expressed in the developing neuroepithelium at E10.5.
source: ISH for Megf8 on E10.5 paraffin sagittal section shows expression in the developing neuroepithelium.
evidence: Shown through ISH in Figure 2F.

claim: Megf8 is expressed throughout the developing nervous system from E11.5 to P0.
source: In situ hybridization on coronal cryosections from E11.5-P0 shows strong Megf8 expression at all time points in the DRG and TG.
evidence: Shown through ISH in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Megf8 is expressed in the hippocampus at P0.
source: In situ hybridization on coronal cryosections at P0 shows strong Megf8 expression in the hippocampus
evidence: Shown through ISH in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Megf8 is expressed in layer 4/5 of the cortex at P0.
source: In situ hybridization on coronal cryosections at P0 shows strong Megf8 expression in layer 4/5 of the cortex
evidence: Shown through ISH in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Megf8 is expressed in the olfactory bulb at P0.
source: In situ hybridization on coronal cryosections at P0 shows strong Megf8 expression in the olfactory bulb
evidence: Shown through ISH in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Megf8 null mutant phenocopies the point mutant Megf8L1775P/L1775P.
source: The Megf8−/− null mutant phenocopies the point mutant Megf8L1775P/L1775P.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount neurofilament staining in Figure 3A.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have limb defects at E13.5 and E16.5.
source: Whole-mount images of Megf8+/+ and Megf8L1775P/L1775P hindlimbs at E13.5 (top) and Megf8+/+ and Megf8L1775P/L1775P forelimbs at E16.5 (bottom).
evidence: Shown through whole-mount imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have a split sternum and delayed ossification of the rib cage.
source: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have a split sternum and delayed ossification of the rib cage.
evidence: Shown through Alcian blue and alizarin red staining in Figure 3C.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have complete left-right inversion of heart looping.
source: Megf8L1775P/L1775P have complete left-right inversion of heart looping.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount imaging of E10.5 hearts in Figure 3D.

claim: Megf8−/− embryos show reversal of embryonic turning and exencephaly.
source: Whole-mount images of E11.5 Megf8+/+ and Megf8−/− littermates, showing reversal of embryonic turning and exencephaly in the Megf8−/−.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount imaging in Figure 3E.

claim: Megf8−/− embryos show severe edema at E13.5.
source: Whole-mount images of Megf8+/+ and Megf8−/− littermates at E13.5, showing severe edema in the Megf8−/−.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount imaging in Figure 3F.

claim: Western blot shows a loss of Megf8 protein in Megf8−/− neurons.
source: Western blot of E12.5 TG and DRG lysates from Megf8+/+, Megf8+/−, and Megf8−/− littermates. The blot was probed with rabbit anti-Megf8 and shows a loss of Megf8 protein in Megf8−/− neurons.
evidence: Shown through Western blot analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have digit duplication and duplication of bones in the hand.
source: Alcian blue staining on E16.5 limbs shows that Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have digit duplication as well as duplication of bones in the hand.
evidence: Shown through Alcian blue staining in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have duplication of the bones of the autopodium.
source: Alizarin red staining on E16.5 limbs shows that Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have duplication of the bones of the autopodium.
evidence: Shown through alizarin red staining in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have a wider and shorter ribcage, delayed ossification of the ribcage, and a split sternum.
source: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutants have a wider and shorter ribcage, delayed ossification of the ribcage, and a split sternum.
evidence: Shown through Alcian blue and alizarin red staining in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutant embryos have missing atrial septum and poorly formed or atretic atrioventricular valves at E15.5.
source: The arrowhead in the control E15.5 embryo section points to the atrial septum; the arrowhead in the mutant embryo section points to the vestige of the endocardial cushion, above which the atrial septum is missing and below which the atrioventricular valves are poorly formed or atretic.
evidence: Shown through H&E staining in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and D.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutant embryos have normal endocardial cushion mesenchyme at E12.5.
source: β-galactosidase and nuclear fast red staining of E12.5 embryos shows normal endocardial cushion (EC) mesenchyme (arrows).
evidence: Shown through β-galactosidase staining in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and E.

claim: Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutant embryos have apparently normal atrioventricular cushion mesenchyme at E10.5.
source: H and E staining of E10.5 control and mutant sections. Note the apparently normal atrioventricular cushion mesenchyme at E10.5 (arrows).
evidence: Shown through H&E staining in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and F.

claim: DRG spinal nerves are undergrown in Megf8−/− embryos at E11.5.
source: Whole-mount neurofilament staining of E11.5 Megf8+/+ and Megf8−/− littermates showing the DRG spinal nerves, which are undergrown in the Megf8−/− (arrow).
evidence: Shown through whole-mount neurofilament staining in Figure 4A and D.

claim: The radial and ulnar nerves are undergrown in Megf8−/− embryos at E13.5.
source: Whole-mount peripherin staining of forelimbs from E13.5 Megf8+/+ and Megf8−/− littermates. The radial and ulnar nerves are undergrown in the Megf8−/− embryo.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount peripherin staining in Figure 4B and E.

claim: The vagus/glossopharyngeal nerves are defasciculated in Megf8−/− embryos at E11.5.
source: Whole-mount neurofilament staining of E11.5 Megf8+/+ and Megf8−/− littermates. The vagus/glossopharyngeal nerves are defasciculated in the Megf8−/− (arrow).
evidence: Shown through whole-mount neurofilament staining in Figure 4C and F.

claim: Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox embryos show defasciculation of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve.
source: Whole-mount neurofilament staining of E11.5 Megf8Flox/Flox and Wnt1-Cre; Megf8Flox/Flox littermates.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount neurofilament staining in Figure 4G.

claim: The number of branches at the nasociliary branch point was significantly greater for Megf8−/−, Megf8L1775P/L1775P, and Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox embryos compared to wild-type.
source: the number of branches at the nasociliary branch point was significantly greater for KO, L1775P, and cKO embryos.
evidence: Shown through quantification in Figure 4H.

claim: The ophthalmic branch was undergrown in Megf8−/−, Megf8L1775P/L1775P, and Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox embryos.
source: the ophthalmic branch was undergrown in KO, L1775P, and cKO embryos.
evidence: Shown through quantification in Figure 4H.

claim: Wnt1-Cre-mediated conditional deletion of Megf8 leads to defasciculation of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve.
source: Wnt1-Cre-mediated conditional deletion of Megf8 leads to defasciculation of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, phenocopying Megf8−/− and Megf8L1775P/L1775P mutant embryos
evidence: Demonstrated through conditional knockout analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Megf8 mediates guidance of developing TG axons in a cell autonomous manner.
source: These findings suggest that Megf8 mediates guidance of developing TG axons in a cell autonomous manner.
evidence: Inferred from Wnt1-Cre conditional knockout experiments showing TG phenotype when Megf8 is deleted in neural crest-derived cells.

claim: Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox embryos do not exhibit a defect in radial/ulnar nerve development.
source: Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox embryos do not exhibit a defect in radial/ulnar nerve development
evidence: Shown through whole-mount peripherin staining in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Megf8's role in spinal nerve axon guidance is non-cell autonomous.
source: Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox embryos do not exhibit a defect in radial/ulnar nerve development, however, suggesting that Megf8's role in spinal nerve axon guidance is non-cell autonomous
evidence: Inferred from the absence of radial/ulnar nerve phenotype in Wnt1-Cre conditional knockouts despite presence of phenotype in full knockouts.

claim: Loss of BMP4 or BMP7 results in pre-axial polydactyly.
source: Bmp4 and Bmp7 loss-of-function mouse lines exhibit pre-axial polydactyly (Dudley et al., 1995; Luo et al., 1995; Dunn et al., 1997; Selever et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bmp4 null embryos display disrupted left-right patterning and loss of normal rightward heart looping.
source: Bmp4 null embryos also display disrupted left-right patterning and loss of normal rightward heart looping (Fujiwara et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujiwara et al., 2002.

claim: Loss of BMP4 or BMPR2 results in a wide range of heart defects including atrial septal defects, ventricular septal defects, atrioventricular septal defects, and abnormal positioning or septation of the outflow tract.
source: Loss of BMP4, or its receptor BMPR2, results in a wide range of heart defects, including atrial septal defects, ventricular septal defects, atrioventricular septal defects, and abnormal positioning or septation of the outflow tract (Jiao et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2004; Beppu et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BMP4 signaling is required for dorsoventral patterning of the TG.
source: Furthermore, BMP4 signaling is required for dorsoventral patterning of the TG (Hodge et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hodge et al., 2007.

claim: Modifying BMP4 expression in the skin leads to changes in the peripheral innervation and survival of sensory neurons.
source: modifying BMP4 expression in the skin leads to changes in the peripheral innervation and survival of sensory neurons (Guha et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guha et al., 2004.

claim: Bmp4 is expressed in the developing craniofacial region at E10.5 and E11.5.
source: Whole-mount β-galactosidase and neurofilament (NFM) co-staining on Bmp4lacZ/+ embryos at E10.5 and E11.5, showing the relationship between Bmp4 expression and the developing TG nerve.
evidence: Shown through β-galactosidase staining in Figure 5A.

claim: Bmp4 expression is lost at the location where defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic nerve occurs in Megf8−/− embryos.
source: Bmp4 expression is lost at the location where defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic nerve occurs in Megf8−/− and Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox embryos.
evidence: Shown through β-galactosidase and neurofilament co-staining in Figure 5B.

claim: The disruption of Bmp4 expression was fully penetrant and observed in all Megf8−/− (n = 4) and Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox (n = 3) embryos assessed.
source: The disruption of Bmp4 expression was fully penetrant and observed in all Megf8−/− (n = 4) and Wnt1-Cre;Megf8Flox/Flox (n = 3) embryos assessed.
evidence: Stated in the figure legend for Figure 5B.

claim: Wnt1-Cre;Bmpr2Flox/− embryos show stunted and prematurely branching ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve at E11.5.
source: the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve in E11.5 Wnt1-Cre;Bmpr2Flox/− embryos is stunted and branches prematurely in a manner reminiscent of the phenotype seen in Megf8 loss-of-function lines
evidence: Shown through whole-mount neurofilament staining in Figure 5C.

claim: The maxillary and mandibular branches of the trigeminal nerve are unaffected in Wnt1-Cre;Bmpr2Flox/− embryos.
source: Furthermore, the maxillary and mandibular branches of the trigeminal nerve are unaffected in the Wnt1-Cre;Bmpr2Flox/− embryos, as in Megf8 null lines.
evidence: Stated in the text describing Figure 5C results.

claim: BMP signaling is required specifically for development of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve.
source: These results demonstrate that BMP signaling is required specifically for development of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve
evidence: Inferred from the selective phenotype in Wnt1-Cre;Bmpr2Flox/− embryos.

claim: Both Megf8 and BMPR2 are necessary to mediate BMP signaling in the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve.
source: they suggest that both Megf8 and BMPR2 are necessary to mediate this signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the similar phenotypes in Megf8 and Bmpr2 mutants.

claim: Bmpr2 is robustly expressed in all three lobes of the developing TG.
source: Bmpr2 is robustly expressed in all three lobes of the developing TG, as is Megf8 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown through in situ hybridization in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bmp4 expression is intact throughout the rest of the Megf8−/− embryo outside the region of TG ophthalmic nerve defasciculation.
source: Bmp4 expression is lost at the location where defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic nerve occurs in Megf8−/− embryos but is intact throughout the rest of the embryo.
evidence: Shown through whole-mount β-galactosidase staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing doses of BMP4 cause robust inhibition of wild-type TG axon outgrowth in vitro.
source: Quantification of (A): axonal outgrowth of wild-type TG explants in the presence of 0–100 ng/ml BMP4. Increasing doses of BMP4 caused robust inhibition of axon outgrowth
evidence: Shown through TG explant assay quantification in Figure 6C.

claim: BMP4 inhibition of axon outgrowth is partially lost in Megf8−/− TG explants.
source: BMP4 inhibition of axon outgrowth is partially lost in Megf8−/− explants
evidence: Shown through TG explant assay quantification in Figure 6D.

claim: Maximal doses of BMP4 inhibit wild-type TG axon outgrowth by more than 50%.
source: BMP4 robustly inhibits the outgrowth of wild-type TG axons, and maximal doses inhibit axon outgrowth by more than 50%
evidence: Shown through TG explant assay results in Figure 6.

claim: TG neurons require Megf8 expression to mediate their maximal response to the inhibitory effects of BMP4.
source: This inhibition was partially lost in Megf8−/− explants, indicating that TG neurons require Megf8 expression to mediate their maximal response to the inhibitory effects of BMP4.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced BMP4 response in Megf8−/− explants compared to controls.

claim: Megf8 is necessary for BMP4 signaling in sensory neurons.
source: These findings suggest that Megf8 is necessary for BMP4 signaling in sensory neurons
evidence: Inferred from the reduced BMP4 response in Megf8−/− TG explants.

claim: BMP4 signaling provides an important inhibitory cue to guide developing TG axons.
source: this signaling provides an important inhibitory cue to guide developing TG axons.
evidence: Inferred from the expression pattern of Bmp4 and the inhibitory effects of BMP4 on TG axon outgrowth.

claim: Bmp4 expression is disrupted in Megf8−/− embryos at the site of defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic branch.
source: our finding that Bmp4 expression is disrupted in Megf8−/− embryos at the site of defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic branch
evidence: Shown through β-galactosidase staining in Figure 5B.

claim: Megf8 may have a non-cell autonomous role in regulating Bmp4 expression.
source: suggests a possible non-cell autonomous role for Megf8 in regulating Bmp4 expression
evidence: Speculated based on the disrupted Bmp4 expression pattern in Megf8 mutants.

claim: BMP4 expression may be dependent on signaling from incoming TG axons, which is disrupted by defasciculation in the Megf8−/− embryo.
source: wherein BMP4 expression is dependent on signaling from incoming TG axons, which is disrupted by defasciculation in the Megf8−/− embryo.
evidence: Proposed as one possible explanation for disrupted Bmp4 expression in Megf8 mutants.

claim: BMP4 may be directly regulated by Megf8 expressed in cells of the craniofacial region.
source: Alternatively, BMP4 may be directly regulated by Megf8 expressed in cells of the craniofacial region.
evidence: Proposed as an alternative explanation for disrupted Bmp4 expression in Megf8 mutants.

claim: It is unlikely that Megf8 predominantly regulates BMP4 signaling through modifying BMP4 expression.
source: Given that Bmp4 expression is preserved in all other areas of the Megf8−/− embryos as well as our in vitro findings that show Megf8 is required in TG neurons to mediate the inhibitory effects of exogenous BMP4, we think it is unlikely that Megf8 predominantly regulates BMP4 signaling through modifying BMP4 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the preserved Bmp4 expression in most areas of Megf8 mutants and the in vitro findings.

claim: Megf8 is expressed in TG sensory neurons where it acts cell autonomously to promote signaling in response to target-derived BMP4.
source: Megf8 is expressed in TG sensory neurons where it acts cell autonomously to promote signaling in response to target-derived BMP4.
evidence: Supported by expression studies, conditional knockout experiments, and in vitro assays.

claim: Megf8-mediated BMP4 signaling is inhibitory for TG axons.
source: Megf8-mediated BMP4 signaling, which is inhibitory for TG axons
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro TG explant assays showing BMP4 inhibition of axon outgrowth.

claim: Megf8-mediated BMP4 signaling enables TG axons to remain fasciculated en route to their appropriate targets in the face.
source: Megf8-mediated BMP4 signaling, which is inhibitory for TG axons, likely enables these axons to remain fasciculated en route to their appropriate targets in the face.
evidence: Inferred from the defasciculation phenotype in Megf8 and Bmpr2 mutants and the inhibitory effects of BMP4.

claim: Disruption of Megf8 or other components of the BMP4 pathway leads to a loss of inhibition and premature defasciculation of the TG ophthalmic nerve.
source: Disruption of this signaling, either through loss of Megf8 or other components of the BMP4 pathway, leads to a corresponding loss of inhibition and premature defasciculation of the nerve.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotypes observed in Megf8 and Bmpr2 mutants.

claim: BMP4 signaling is required for TG axon guidance.
source: Thus, BMP4 signaling is required for TG axon guidance
evidence: Demonstrated through Bmpr2 conditional knockout experiments and in vitro assays.

claim: Megf8 is a novel component of BMP4 signaling in TG sensory neurons.
source: Megf8 is a novel component of BMP4 signaling in TG sensory neurons.
evidence: Supported by genetic, expression, and functional studies showing Megf8's role in mediating BMP4 effects on TG neurons.

claim: Megf8 mediates signaling by BMP4 and, perhaps, other TGFβ family members throughout the embryo during development.
source: we propose that Megf8 mediates signaling by BMP4 and, perhaps, other TGFβ family members throughout the embryo during development.
evidence: Proposed based on the numerous phenotypic similarities between Megf8 and Bmp loss-of-function mouse lines.

claim: Mutations in Megf8 were identified in a small subset of children with Carpenter syndrome.
source: mutations in Megf8 were recently identified in a small subset of children with Carpenter syndrome, which is an autosomal-recessive multiple-congenital-malformation disorder.
evidence: Supported by citation to Twigg et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations in Megf8 in Carpenter syndrome patients resulted in thoracic skeletal defects, limb defects such as pre-axial polydactyly, congenital heart defects, and profound lateralization defects.
source: Mutations were identified in several domains of Megf8, including the Kelch domain adjacent to the Kelch domain harboring the L1775P point mutation, and resulted in thoracic skeletal defects, limb defects such as pre-axial polydactyly, congenital heart defects, and profound lateralization defects including transposition of the great arteries, dextrocardia, and complete situs inversus (Twigg et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Twigg et al., 2012.

claim: Phenotypes in Carpenter syndrome patients with Megf8 mutations mirror those seen in Megf8 loss-of-function mouse lines.
source: These phenotypes mirror those seen in our Megf8 loss-of-function lines and reinforce the vital role for Megf8 throughout embryogenesis.
evidence: Comparison between human Carpenter syndrome phenotypes and mouse Megf8 mutant phenotypes.

claim: Loss of Megf8 function leads to embryonic lethality by age E16.5.
source: These phenotypes were seen in all embryos at E14.5 or later, and they lead to severe peripheral edema (Figure 3F) and embryonic lethality by age E16.5.
evidence: Observed through analysis of Megf8 mutant embryos at different developmental stages.

claim: Megf8 mutant embryos have apparently normal endocardial cushion mesenchymal cells at early stages.
source: Analysis at earlier stages revealed apparently normal endocardial cushion mesenchymal cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Shown through histological analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The terminal heart pathologies in Megf8 mutants result from improper remodeling events after E12.5.
source: which implies that the terminal pathologies result from improper remodeling events after E12.5.
evidence: Inferred from the normal appearance of endocardial cushion mesenchyme at early stages but severe defects at later stages.

claim: Conditional mutation of the Megf8Flox allele using the Mesp1-Cre line did not cause any heart phenotypes.
source: Conditional mutation of the Megf8Flox allele using the Mesp1-Cre line (Saga et al., 1999), which is active in all mesoderm of the heart, did not cause any heart phenotypes (data not shown)
evidence: Stated as unpublished observation.

claim: Early heart and embryo laterality defects might be responsible for the constellation of later heart defects in Megf8 mutants.
source: implying that early heart and embryo laterality defects might be responsible for the constellation of later heart defects.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of heart phenotypes in Mesp1-Cre conditional knockouts.

claim: A second mouse line harboring a Megf8 point mutation (Megf8C193R) was identified in an independent forward genetic screen.
source: These findings are consistent with a second mouse line harboring a Megf8 point mutation (Megf8C193R) that was identified in an independent forward genetic screen
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: The Megf8C193R mouse line has polydactyly and defects in left-right patterning and heart development.
source: which was shown to have polydactyly and defects in left-right patterning and heart development (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009.
